findings.issue: Source opens "Alexandria, also called Paris, challenges Menelaus"; candidate has "Paris challenges Menelaus". The double-name gloss is dropped, which is consistent with the STYLE-NOTE rule that Alexandrus is written Paris (recorded in ACCEPTANCE-RECORD.md). No fix needed.

Source: "Did you not, such as you are, get your following together and sail beyond the seas?" Candidate: "Is this what you were when you gathered your followers and sailed over the seas?" This changes the rhetorical question into a different, less clear one (what you were then), and the next sentence then repeats "being what you are". Restore the source question.
findings.fix: Then Hector scolded him. “Paris,” he said, “you evil-hearted Paris, so fair to look at, so mad for women, such a liar. I wish you had never been born, or had died unmarried. That would be better than living to be disgraced and looked at sideways. Will the Achaeans not mock us? They will say we sent a champion who is fair to look at but has no brains and no courage. Did you not, being what you are, gather your followers and sail over the seas? Did you not, from a far country, carry off a lovely woman married among a people of warriors—bringing sorrow to your father, your city and your whole country, joy to your enemies, and a hang-dog shame to yourself? And now you do not dare face Menelaus and find out what kind of man he is, whose wife you have stolen? Where would your lyre be then, and your love-tricks, your handsome locks and your fair looks, when you were lying in the dust in front of him? The Trojans are a weak-kneed people. Otherwise you would long ago have been given a shirt of stones for the wrongs you have done them.”

findings.issue: Source: "Ulysses, on the other hand, when he rose to speak, was at first silent and kept his eyes fixed upon the ground." Candidate: "Odysseus, on the other hand, was silent when he rose to speak, and at first kept his eyes fixed on the ground." "At first" has moved from the silence to the downcast eyes, so the silence no longer reads as temporary.
findings.fix: Antenor then said, “Madam, you have spoken truly. Odysseus once came here as an envoy about you, and Menelaus came with him. I received them in my own house, so I know both of them by sight and by conversation. When they stood up before the assembled Trojans, Menelaus had the broader shoulders, but when both were seated Odysseus looked the more royal. After a time they delivered their message. The speech of Menelaus ran trippingly off the tongue. He did not say much, being a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point, though he was the younger of the two. Odysseus, on the other hand, when he rose to speak, was at first silent and kept his eyes fixed on the ground. He made no play or graceful movement with his scepter. He held it straight and stiff, like a man unpracticed in oratory, and you might have taken him for a mere churl or simpleton. But when he raised his voice and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, no one could touch him, and nobody thought any more about how he looked.”
